title: Follicular Lymphoma
subject: Pathology
summary: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent B‑cell non‑Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by nodular growth and BCL2 over‑expression due to t(14;18). It presents with painless lymphadenopathy and may transform to aggressive disease.

sections.p: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a germinal‑centre B‑cell neoplasm with a nodular architecture. Diagnosis requires histology showing a mixture of centrocytes and centroblasts and confirmation of the t(14;18) translocation or BCL2 over‑expression.
b: Nodular pattern on excisional lymph node biopsy
Centrocytes (small cleaved cells) dominate; ≤5 centroblasts/HPF = grade 1, 6‑15 = grade 2, >15 = grade 3
Immunophenotype: CD20+, CD10+, BCL2+, BCL6+, Ki‑67 low

t.b: Confirms histologic grade and architecture; essential for definitive diagnosis

t.a: FISH for t(14;18) or PCR for IGH‑BCL2
t.b: Detects the hallmark translocation; if unavailable, rely on immunohistochemistry for BCL2

t.a: Flow cytometry of fine‑needle aspirate (if biopsy not feasible)
t.b: Shows clonal CD19+/CD20+ B‑cells with light‑chain restriction; supports diagnosis when tissue not accessible

sections.p: Staging follows the Ann Ann Arbor system (I–IV) and the FL International Prognostic Index (FLIPI) predicts outcome.
b: Ann Ann Arbor stage based on nodal/extranodal sites and systemic symptoms
FLIPI factors: age > 60, hemoglobin < 12 g/dL, LDH ↑, >4 nodal sites, stage III/IV

t.a: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (or ultrasound where CT unavailable)
t.b: Assigns Ann Ann Arbor stage; if imaging not possible, clinical exam and chest X‑ray give approximate stage

t.a: Baseline labs (CBC, LDH, β2‑microglobulin, hepatitis B/C serology)
t.b: Provides FLIPI variables; guides risk‑adapted therapy

sections.p: FL arises from acquired genetic events; the dominant cause is the t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation leading to BCL2 over‑expression. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing infections (HIV, hepatitis B) can accelerate disease or affect treatment choices.
b: t(14;18) translocation → BCL2 over‑expression (apoptosis resistance)
Chronic immune stimulation (e.g., HIV infection)
Environmental factors: pesticide exposure, chronic antigenic drive

t.b: Identifies co‑infection that may alter prognosis and dictate antiretroviral therapy before chemotherapy

sections.p: Patients usually have painless, generalized lymphadenopathy. B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) are less common early but may appear with higher grade or transformation.
b: Enlarged, non‑tender peripheral nodes
Occasional splenomegaly
Rarely, extranodal masses (e.g., gastrointestinal polyps)

sections.p: A stepwise approach balances diagnostic certainty with resource constraints.
b: Physical exam for nodal distribution and organomegaly
Basic labs: CBC, LDH, liver/renal function

t.b: Detects splenomegaly or intra‑abdominal nodes when CT unavailable
Assesses marrow involvement; required for staging if peripheral blood shows cytopenias
Defines metabolic activity, helps detect transformation; if not available, rely on CT and clinical assessment

sections.p: Rapid nodal growth, new B symptoms, or laboratory evidence of transformation demand urgent reassessment.
b: Transformation to diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
Hyperviscosity from high tumor burden
Severe cytopenias from marrow infiltration

sections.p: Therapy is risk‑adapted. Low‑grade, asymptomatic disease may be observed; symptomatic or high‑risk disease requires immunochemotherapy.
b: Watch‑and‑wait for stage I–II, grade 1–2, no B symptoms
R‑CHOP (rituximab + cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) for symptomatic or high‑grade disease
R‑CVP (rituximab + cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone) when anthracycline toxicity is a concern

t.b: Targets CD20 on B‑cells; essential for all chemo‑regimens; avoid in active hepatitis B without prophylaxis
Alkylating agent; preferred over doxorubicin if cardiac disease or limited monitoring of cardiac function

t.a: Supportive care – growth factor (G‑CSF) if neutropenia risk high, prophylactic antibiotics in HIV
t.b: Reduces infection risk; G‑CSF use guided by ANC < 500 µL

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects relapse or transformation.
b: Clinical review every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then 6–12 months
CBC, LDH, and physical exam at each visit
Repeat imaging (ultrasound or CT) if new symptoms or rising LDH

sections.p: Several indolent lymphomas share nodular patterns.
b: Mantle‑cell lymphoma – cyclin D1 positivity, t(11;14)
Nodular lymphocyte‑predominant Hodgkin lymphoma – CD20+, CD15‑, CD30‑
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia – diffuse pattern, CD5+

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite active disease.
b: LDH can be normal in low‑grade FL; do not rely on it alone for staging
Peripheral blood may lack circulating lymphoma cells; marrow biopsy still required if suspicion high

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in node size, new B symptoms, or rapid rise in LDH – possible transformation
Severe cytopenias causing infection or bleeding

faq.q: Why is rituximab used in all regimens?
faq.a: It binds CD20, depleting malignant B‑cells and improves response rates without adding significant organ toxicity.
It is generally incurable but highly controllable; long‑term remission is common with appropriate therapy.
In asymptomatic, low‑grade disease without bulky nodes or organ compromise, observation avoids unnecessary toxicity.

exam: A 45‑year‑old with painless cervical nodes and no B symptoms – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Excisional node biopsy to obtain histology and grade; fine‑needle aspirate is insufficient.
How does the t(14;18) translocation drive follicular lymphoma pathogenesis? — It places BCL2 under the IGH enhancer, causing over‑expression of an anti‑apoptotic protein.
A patient on R‑CHOP develops rising transaminases – which drug is most likely responsible and what should you do? — Doxorubicin is hepatotoxic; consider dose reduction or switch to R‑CVP.

What features on histology distinguish grade 3 follicular lymphoma from transformed DLBCL? — Grade 3 has >15 centroblasts/HPF but retains follicular architecture; DLBCL shows diffuse sheets of large cells.

In a low‑resource clinic without PET‑CT, how would you assess for transformation? — Rely on rapid clinical deterioration, new B symptoms, rising LDH, and repeat CT or ultrasound plus repeat biopsy of the most suspicious node.

Why is anthracycline (doxorubicin) avoided in patients with limited cardiac monitoring? — It can cause irreversible cardiomyopathy; without echocardiography you should use anthracycline‑free regimens.

How does HIV infection modify the management of follicular lymphoma? — Requires antiretroviral therapy, prophylaxis for hepatitis B reactivation, and may favor less intensive chemo due to immunosuppression.
What red‑flag laboratory change suggests transformation to aggressive lymphoma? — Sudden LDH rise > 2 × upper limit of normal or new cytopenias.
